catalog_quote: 4.3.5 Tone as a tense contrastive marker. As we have seen in the previous sections, tone plays a significant role in the T/A system of Leki and some Bantu languages. In Leki, this can be observed on the use of either high tone or low tone on different elements of the verb template. new_statements.rule_in_words: The only accessible first-hand description treats Kara (Leki) as a tone language with High, Low and rise-fall tones whose placement on the verb distinguishes tense/aspect categories; it makes no statement at all about word stress or accent position, so no stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the work is about tense/aspect, and tone is discussed only as a T/A contrast (present retrospective vs remote past; progressive marker; habitual present vs past habitual pronouns).
new_statements.domain_note: Verb-word level tone contrasts in elicited sentences (inland Leki of Nyang'ombe village, Ukara Island); no treatment of nouns, citation forms, phrase-level prosody or penultimate lengthening.
new_statements.identity_note: Masatu 2015 describes 'Leki' (autonym Shíleki; island name Kwileki = Ukara), explicitly equated with Kara/Regi, Maho JE.252 (p. 3-4) = Glottolog kara1481 [reg]; data from inland Leki (Nyang'ombe village), which the author distinguishes from a Jita-influenced 'Lakeside Leki'. Magesa 2017 'Kikara' data are from Bukiko and Nyamanga wards, Ukerewe district (same language). Not to be confused with Kara of Ethiopia (Omotic), Kara of CAR (kara1482) or Kara of PNG (leu), which dominate web results.

sources.locator: section 4.3.5 'Tone as a tense contrastive marker', pp. 69-70 (PDF pp. 86-87); tone symbols p. viii; language identity p. 3
sources.note: Nothing on word stress/accent. Treats Leki (=Kara/Regi) as tonal: symbols list High, Low and Rise-fall tone; section 4.3.5 'Tone as a tense contrastive marker' (pp. 69-70) shows H vs L tone on the verb template distinguishing present retrospective from remote past (Na-ta-ile 'I have already tapped' vs Na-ta-ile low-toned 'I tapped (remote past)'), high tone on the progressive marker and on past-habitual pronouns. The only occurrence of 'stress' is a comparison to English auto-stressed suffixes (p. 66).

sources.note: Silent: no mention of mkazo (stress) or of a Kikara tone/accent system; 'toni' appears only in the literature review about other Bantu languages (Nurse 2008 examples). Data from Bukiko and Nyamanga wards, Ukerewe district; Kikara verb forms given without tone marks.
